back: 1. [[kw:Observational study]] – observe without interfering.
2. [[kw:Experiment]] – apply a treatment and compare results.
3. [[kw:Simulation]] – use a model to imitate reality.
4. [[kw:Survey]] – ask questions to a sample.
[[imp:Choose the method based on the study's goal.]]
cards.front: What are the four main methods of [[kw:data collection]]?

back: A researcher [[imp:observes and measures characteristics]] but does [[imp:NOT]] change existing conditions.
No treatment is applied.
Example: recording how often children put non‑food objects in their mouths.
A [[imp:treatment is applied]] to one group, and responses are compared to a [[imp:control group]].
The control group may receive a [[kw:placebo]] (a fake treatment).
Example: testing a new allergy drug vs. a placebo.
A [[imp:mathematical or physical model]] reproduces a real‑world situation.
Used when actual study is [[imp:impractical, dangerous, or expensive]].
Example: crash test dummies in car safety tests.
An investigation that [[imp:asks questions]] to a sample of a population.
Can be done by interview, mail, or phone.
[[imp:Wording must be neutral to avoid bias.]]
1. [[kw:Control]] – limit outside variables; use a control group.
2. [[kw:Randomization]] – randomly assign subjects to treatment groups.
3. [[kw:Replication]] – use enough subjects (large sample size) to confirm results.
[[imp:Missing any element weakens the experiment.]]
cards.front: What are the three key elements of a well‑designed [[kw:experiment]]?

back: An outside factor that [[imp:makes it impossible to tell]] which variable caused the effect.
Example: A coffee shop remodels with bright colors at the same time a new mall opens; increased business could be due to either.
[[imp:Avoid confounding by changing only one variable at a time.]]
[[kw:Blinding]]: subjects don't know if they get the real treatment or a placebo.
[[kw:Double‑blind]]: [[imp:neither the subjects nor the experimenters know]] who gets what, until data collection is complete.
Both techniques reduce the [[imp:placebo effect]] and [[imp:experimenter bias]].
Every member of the population has an [[imp:equal chance]] of being selected.
Every possible sample of the same size also has an equal chance.
Often implemented with a random number table or generator.
Divide the population into subgroups ([[kw:strata]]) that share a characteristic.
Then take a [[imp:random sample from each stratum]].
Ensures each subgroup is represented.
Example: sampling students by grade level (freshman, sophomore, etc.).
Divide the population into [[imp:naturally occurring clusters]] (e.g., zip codes, classrooms).
Randomly select one or more clusters and include [[imp:all members]] from those clusters.
[[imp:Clusters should be similar to each other.]]
Assign numbers, choose a random start, then select every k‑th member.
Example: testing every 50th light bulb on an assembly line.
[[imp:Easy to use, but can be biased if a pattern exists in the data.]]

cards.front: What is a [[kw:convenience sample]] and why is it biased?
back: A sample taken from [[imp:easily available]] members of the population.
Example: surveying only people walking by a booth.
[[imp:Not representative]] — often leads to biased results.
Subjects are first divided into [[kw:blocks]] based on a characteristic (e.g., age, gender).
Then, [[imp:within each block, subjects are randomly assigned]] to treatments.
Controls for the blocking variable.
Similar to stratified sampling, but for experiments.
Subjects are [[imp:paired up based on similarity]] (e.g., identical twins, or the same person before/after).
One in each pair gets treatment A, the other gets treatment B.
Reduces variability by [[imp:controlling for individual differences]].
